description:
Space exploration is more than launching rockets into space. The Space Mission Design Game challenges participants to step into the role of space mission designers and experience the process of planning, building, and managing a complete space mission.

The goal is to create an interactive and engaging experience that transforms complex space engineering concepts into practical learning through simulation, experimentation, and decision-making.
summary:
Mission Frontier is an interactive space mission design simulator that allows students to experience the process of planning, designing and managing a space mission. It was developed to make the engineering decisions behind space exploration easier to understand through practical experimentation.

Users can choose from four mission scenarios — Mars, Moon, Asteroid and Earth — and work through different stages of a mission. They define scientific objectives, design a spacecraft by selecting its architecture and components, and evaluate constraints involving mass, power, budget and propulsion. They can also plan mission routes, explore orbital parameters, build mission timelines and manage unexpected situations through Mission Control.

The simulation connects these decisions to mission readiness and performance. At the end, users receive a mission report that reviews their choices, results and areas for improvement.

Mission Frontier uses scientific reference parameters and simplified educational assumptions to demonstrate how engineering decisions influence a mission. Its aim is to help students understand the planning and trade-offs involved in designing a space mission.
details:
Project Overview

Mission Frontier is a browser-based space mission design and simulation platform developed to help students understand what goes into planning and managing a space mission. In a real mission, decisions about the spacecraft, scientific instruments, power, propulsion, communication and orbital path are closely connected. We wanted to create an environment where students could explore these decisions and see how they affect the mission as a whole.

The platform offers four mission scenarios: Mars, Moon, Asteroid and Earth. Each scenario gives users a starting point for designing their own mission and exploring different engineering choices.

How the Platform Works

The experience begins with selecting a mission and reviewing its scientific objectives. Users then move to the Spacecraft Designer, where they choose a spacecraft architecture and select components for their design. During this stage, they work with parameters such as launch mass, power consumption, propulsion requirements, propellant and budget.

An engineering dashboard helps users review their design, while validation checks identify issues that may affect mission readiness. Users can also adjust scenario inputs and component operating conditions to understand how different configurations affect the spacecraft.

After spacecraft design, users move to mission planning and orbital planning. The route planner allows them to configure mission-related choices, while the orbit planner introduces concepts such as circular orbital velocity and orbital period. These calculations use standard orbital mechanics equations for supported cases. Users then create a mission timeline by arranging mission phases and assigning durations to them.

The next stage is Mission Control. Here, users progress through their planned mission and respond to simulated events. These can include reduced solar power, communication interruptions, instrument problems and navigation corrections. Their decisions affect the mission's performance. Once the simulation is complete, a mission report presents the results, score breakdown and engineering observations.

Engineering and Scientific Concepts

Mission Frontier brings several engineering topics into one workflow. The spacecraft design stage considers mass, power and propulsion requirements. The orbital planner uses gravitational parameters and planetary radii for supported destinations to perform basic orbital calculations. The timeline and simulation stages introduce mission duration, operational planning and responses to unexpected situations.

We have also tried to keep scientific information separate from simplified game inputs. Some parameters use scientific reference values, while others, such as budgets, operating conditions and certain scenario inputs, are educational assumptions. When a required physical parameter is unavailable, the platform allows participants to define it instead of presenting an invented value as a scientific fact. This distinction is important because the purpose is to teach engineering trade-offs without suggesting that every game value represents a real spacecraft specification.

Creativity, Benefits and Intended Impact

One of our main design choices was to connect the different stages of a mission instead of treating spacecraft design, orbital mechanics and mission operations as separate activities. For example, users must consider spacecraft resources during design and then manage the mission through its later stages. The simulation gives them a chance to try different choices and understand why a particular design may work well or face difficulties.

Mission Frontier is intended mainly for students and beginners interested in space science and engineering. It provides a way to experiment with mission planning, resource management and basic orbital concepts without needing access to an actual spacecraft or laboratory.

Through this project, we hope students will gain a clearer understanding of the decisions involved in space exploration and become more interested in the engineering behind future missions.
